query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for structural use under extreme-temperature conditions, what single intervention could improve high-temperature oxygen resistance? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the untreated alloy, defines the temperature, atmosphere, and exposure conditions under which it should work, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of chromium to refractory high-entropy alloys will improve their high-temperature oxygen resistance by forming a protective oxide layer.
generation.conditions: high-temperature conditions in an oxidizing atmosphere
generation.structural_mediator: formation of a protective oxide layer
generation.mechanism: alloying elements affect oxide formation and adhesion
generation.boundary: high-temperature conditions in an oxidizing atmosphere
generation.uncertainty: the exact amount of chromium addition and the resulting oxide layer formation

falsification_experiment.design: expose chromium-added refractory high-entropy alloys to high-temperature conditions in an oxidizing atmosphere and measure their oxygen resistance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the oxygen resistance of the chromium-added alloys is not improved, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Oxidation resistance is one of the most important properties of high- and medium-entropy alloys and has been studied by many groups. Generally, the addition of Al, Si, and Cr elements in the alloy will significantly enhance the oxidation resistance of the alloy. For example, Sudeep et al. [] and Chen et al. [] proposed that the addition of Al and Cr elements helps AlCoCrFeNi2 and Al0.6CrFeCoNiSiX (X = 0, 0.3) high-entropy alloys to form a continuous oxide layer, which inhibits further oxidation. The addition of Si helps to promote the formation of a continuous oxide layer, which has a positive effect on the antioxidant behavior. The addition of V, Mo, and Ti elements will reduce the oxidation resistance of the substrate, which is not conducive to the improvement of the oxidation resistance of high-entropy alloys. For example, Cao et al. [] realized that Al addition resulted in better oxidation resistance by forming a protective oxide scale, but Mo addition weakened its protective effect. Lu et al.
